newsitem.title: GERMANY: German shops rush to open late as 40-year law goes.
newsitem.headline: German shops rush to open late as 40-year law goes.

text.p: Germany's shops will at last be able to stay open late starting November 1, when a liberalised shop hours law replaces tight restrictions left over from the 1950s.
Both retailers and shop unions had long opposed the change, saying it would wipe out traditional corner shops, spoil workers' free time and upset family life.

But now, surveys show about three-quarters of shops will take the chance to open until eight p.m. on weekdays and four p.m. on Saturdays. The old weekday closing time was 6.30 p.m., with late closings on Thursday, and two p.m. on Saturdays.
However, effects from the new hours will not be immediately obvious because on November 1, a Friday, shops will be shut in Catholic regions of Germany for the All Saints Day holiday.

Even beyond that day though, retailers hold only modest hopes of boosting their turnover with longer hours, and most think big store chains that lobbied for the change will end up taking a larger slice of the retail pie away from local shops.
"I don't believe there will be a miraculous multiplication of money in people's wallets," said Holger Wenzel, head of the German Retailers Association (HDE).
In more service-oriented countries, like the U.S. or Britain, with competitive retail sectors, posters would likely be plastered on storefronts to lure shoppers during later hours.
Not so in Cologne. A walk down the Schildergasse, Germany's fourth busiest shopping street, revealed only a few small notices saying shops would observe the new closing times.
"We're not planning a promotion drive," Thomas Raeder of the City Marketing Cologne group told Reuters. "Total turnover won't rise. There will be just winners and losers."

But he said central Cologne retailers, which include department stores like Metro AG's Kaufhof, Karstadt and recently-opened Marks & Spencer, still hoped to win business by sticking to common opening times.
On Neusser Street, a typical busy shopping street with a full range of local stores in a Cologne suburb, owners have not agreed to coordinate opening hours to win passing trade.
The laundry will still shut at 6.30 p.m. and the optician has has not made up its mind to open later.
And coffee shop manager Christa Schooss said she might stay open late three days a week but does not relish the prospect of a late walk to the metro. "Crime will just rise," she said.

Despite mixed feelings from retailers about the possibility of longer shop hours, Munich-based Ifo institute said in a report "Shop owners should not expect their readiness to adapt to be rewarded with higher turnover straight away. But over the long term longer hours will encourage consumers to spend more."

And consumers, long-suffering victims of bad service who see shopping as one of life's most stressful tasks, will welcome the chance to shop outside normal work times. The longer hours could ultimately unleash pent-up demand, which has been diverted to spending on other consumption like holidays or leisure.

In a recent cover story, entitled "Service Desert Germany", news magazine Focus published a litany of cases of surly staff, sloppy after-sales service and store owners more interested in turning a quick profit than winning loyal customers.
The survey found that just 14 percent of people said they were "very happy" or "quite happy" with shop service.
But store unions, who led Germany's three million shop workers in lightning strikes over the summer to win time off for extra late shifts, warned staffing will be spread more thinly.
"The thinner staff cover will mean that service won't be better, but worse," Margret Moenig-Raane of the HBV trade, banking and insurance unon said.
